abstract.t: This document specifies GSS-SSHKEY, a GSS-API security mechanism that establishes a security context using SSH public keys. The mechanism performs an ephemeral key exchange, authenticates the acceptor with an SSH host key, authenticates the initiator with an SSH user key, and derives per-message keys for GSS-API protection.
This is an experimental specification. The mechanism OID used here is allocated from a private enterprise arc for implementation experiments and is not suitable for final publication.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Overview
section.t: GSS-SSHKEY is a peer authentication and key establishment protocol for the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) . It reuses SSH public-key identities and signature algorithms while presenting the result as an ordinary GSS-API security context.

The initiator is the user side of the exchange. The acceptor is the service or host side. The acceptor proves possession of a trusted SSH host private key. After a shared session secret can be derived, the initiator proves possession of an SSH user private key in an encrypted user-authentication payload. Both peers then prove knowledge of the derived session key.

Context-establishment token values are DER encodings of the ASN.1 SshKeyToken type defined in . The initial initiator token is encapsulated as specified below. Per-message tokens use the GSS-API CFX token framing described in , with keys derived by this mechanism instead of by Kerberos.

section.name: Names and Credentials
section.t: The target name supplied to gss_init_sec_context() SHOULD be a host-based service name. The service component identifies the application service, and the host component identifies the SSH host key namespace in which the acceptor key is validated.

The canonical acceptor name is the service component, an at sign, and the effective destination hostname after client configuration resolution. The hostname is converted to lowercase and a trailing root dot is removed. This value is carried as acceptorName and is bound into host authentication, user authentication, and key confirmation.

The username field in SshKeyUserAuth is the requested local account selected by application or SSH client configuration. Successful key authorization authenticates that account, and the accepted GSS source name and its display form are the exact username octets. The SSH key proves authorization for the account; its fingerprint is not the GSS source name.

The exported name is the RFC 2743 exported-name token for this mechanism OID with the username as the mechanism name payload. gss_localname() and gss_authorize_localname() therefore map and authorize that same requested account name.

The acceptor credential consists of one or more SSH host private keys and their public-key metadata. The initiator credential consists of SSH user keys available through an SSH agent. A GSS mechanism implementation normally cannot prompt for SSH private-key passphrases, so initiator implementations of this mechanism MUST NOT depend on direct user interaction to unlock private key files.

An implementation MUST define how trusted acceptor host public keys are found. Implementations MUST support OpenSSH known_hosts style host-key databases and MUST support SSHFP DNS resource records. SSHFP records MUST be treated as authentic only when the DNS answer is DNSSEC validated. A deployment MAY additionally use a certificate authority or another local trust store. This protocol does not make unauthenticated host keys trustworthy.

section.name: Authorization and Network Identity
section.t: The GSS-API context-establishment interface does not provide this mechanism with an authenticated network hostname or address for the initiator. Address fields supplied as GSS channel bindings bind application-provided values to the context; they do not define those values as initiator authorization identities.

The initiator MAY use the target name and client configuration to select the destination hostname and host-key policy. The acceptor MAY use its own local hostname while parsing local configuration. Neither value is the initiator's hostname at the acceptor.

An acceptor implementing this profile MUST NOT use a DNS hostname for the initiator in an authorization decision. It MUST NOT obtain such a name through reverse DNS, accept one asserted by the initiator, or treat a numeric peer address as a hostname. If local authorization policy depends on an initiator hostname, authentication MUST fail closed for that policy rather than treating the condition as unmatched.

An embedding application MAY provide a numeric source address that its transport observed for the connection through a local implementation interface. Address-dependent authorization policy MAY be evaluated only when that address is available. If it is not available and the result could affect authorization, authentication MUST fail closed.

section.name: Token Encoding
section.t: Every SshKeyToken value is DER encoded. When the initiator begins an exchange, its first token MUST be wrapped in the InitialContextToken framing from Section 3.1 of for this mechanism OID. An initiator responding to an acceptor-first token and all subsequent tokens send raw DER. Implementations MUST reject malformed framing and values that are not valid DER encodings of SshKeyToken.

Algorithm-list fields are OCTET STRING values containing SSH name-lists as defined by . Algorithm name fields are OCTET STRING values containing one SSH algorithm name. Signature blobs are encoded as SSH binary strings as used by and .
EncSshKeyUserAuth and EncCtx.encPart contain the profile ciphertext C followed immediately by its 16-octet integrity checksum H:

These fields do not repeat the negotiated enctype and do not carry an explicit nonce. The profile prepends a random 16-octet confounder to the DER plaintext before encryption. The field-specific labels and key derivation are defined in .

section.name: Algorithm Negotiation
section.t: The kextypes, enctypes, and sigtypes fields carry the initiator's supported key-exchange, encryption, and SSH signature algorithms. The acceptor selects one key-exchange and encryption algorithm, and returns its own sigtypes list naming the user signature algorithms it is willing to verify. The actual host and user signature algorithms are carried in hostauth.sigtype and SshKeyUserAuth.sigtype.
SSH public key type and SSH signature type are negotiated separately. This is necessary for RSA, where one ssh-rsa public key can produce rsa-sha2-512, rsa-sha2-256, or legacy ssh-rsa signatures.

Implementations of this version MUST support curve25519-sha256 for key exchange and aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 for encrypted fields and per-message tokens. They SHOULD support ssh-ed25519 for signatures. Curve25519 is described in . The encryption profile is based on as specified below.
This mechanism is new and has no compatibility requirement for Kerberos DES, Triple-DES, RC4, or other legacy RFC 4121 encryption types.

section.name: Signature Transcripts and Key Schedule
section.t: canonical-channel-bindings is a deterministic encoding of the GSS channel bindings supplied by the application. No channel bindings are encoded as the single octet 0x00. A present channel-binding structure is encoded as:
section.sourcecode: 0x01 || uint32le(initiator-address-type) || uint32le(length(initiator-address)) || initiator-address || uint32le(acceptor-address-type) || uint32le(length(acceptor-address)) || acceptor-address || uint32le(length(application-data)) || application-data
section.t: This field order and little-endian integer encoding follow the channel-binding hash input defined by . Zero-valued lengths are included. The leading presence octet distinguishes no bindings from a present structure with empty buffers. An implementation MUST reject a component whose length cannot be represented in 32 bits. The same canonical value MUST be supplied on every call for one local context; a change MUST fail with GSS_S_BAD_BINDINGS. GSS_C_CHANNEL_BOUND_FLAG is set only after a present structure has been used by a successfully established context.
Signature inputs are encoded as SSH strings as defined by . In the initiator-first flow, the host signature input is:
section.sourcecode: SSH-string("gss-sshkey hostauth v1") || SSH-string(mechanism-oid-der-contents) || SSH-string(kex-algorithm) || SSH-string(encryption-algorithm) || SSH-string(initiator-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(acceptor-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(initiator-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(acceptor-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(initiator-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-name) || SSH-string(canonical-channel-bindings)
section.t: In the acceptor-first flow, the host challenge signature input is:
section.sourcecode: SSH-string("gss-sshkey hostchallenge v1") || SSH-string(mechanism-oid-der-contents) || SSH-string(kex-algorithm) || SSH-string(encryption-algorithm) || SSH-string(acceptor-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(acceptor-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(acceptor-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-name) || SSH-string(canonical-channel-bindings)
section.t: The user signature input is:
section.sourcecode: SSH-string("gss-sshkey userauth v1") || SSH-string(mechanism-oid-der-contents) || SSH-string(kex-algorithm) || SSH-string(encryption-algorithm) || SSH-string(initiator-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(acceptor-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(initiator-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(acceptor-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(initiator-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-name) || SSH-string(username) || SSH-string(user-public-key-type) || SSH-string(user-public-key-blob) || SSH-string(user-signature-algorithm) || SSH-string(canonical-channel-bindings)
section.t: EncSshKeyUserAuth is not tied to a single final user-authentication step. It MAY appear in any token sent after the sender has enough ECDH material to derive K_base. The encrypted payload lets initiator-first exchanges keep the username and user public key confidential from passive observers without adding a round trip.

Let Z be the raw shared secret produced by the selected key exchange. The anonymous ECDH profile derives the base session key with the same SP800-108 HMAC-SHA256 counter-mode KDF inputs as Heimdal SAnon-X25519:
section.sourcecode: K_base = KDF( K1 = Z, label = "sanon-x25519", context = initiator-pk || acceptor-pk || uint32(0) || uint32(flags) || canonical-channel-bindings, L = 128 )
section.t: This version sends no SAnon-style optional protocol flags, so flags is zero. K_base is the 128-bit protocol key for the RFC 8009 AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA256-128 profile. Per-message encryption and integrity keys are derived from it using the RFC 8009 key-usage constants selected by the RFC 4121 sender role and token operation.

Private encrypted fields use the same AES and HMAC primitives with the fixed RFC 4121 initiator-seal key usage 24. Let label be "SSHKEY userauth v1" for EncSshKeyUserAuth or "SSHKEY server context v1" for sctx. Their 128-bit profile keys are:
section.sourcecode:
K_userauth = first-128-bits(HMAC-SHA-256( HMAC-SHA-256(K_base, "SSHKEY userauth v1"), "SSHKEY userauth v1"))
K_sctx = first-128-bits(HMAC-SHA-256( K_context, "SSHKEY server context v1"))
section.t: K_context is a local 256-bit acceptor context-protection key shared by acceptor processes that consume sctx. It is not derived from or sent to the peer. For either field, RFC 8009 derives Ke with constant 0x00000018AA and Ki with constant 0x0000001855. Encryption applies AES CBC ciphertext stealing to a fresh random 16-octet confounder followed by the DER plaintext. The profile's integrity input is label || 16 zero octets || C, extending RFC 8009 with the field label as associated data. H is the first 128 bits of HMAC-SHA-256 under Ki.

Key confirmation uses a finished key derived from K_base and the transcript hash. SshKeyFinished.mac is an HMAC over a role label, the transcript hash, and the peer nonce. This proves possession of the ECDH-derived session key and does not require an additional SSH signature or SSH agent operation.
A user-authentication retry uses a distinct transcript hash:
section.sourcecode: SHA-256( SSH-string("gss-sshkey userauth retry v1") || SSH-string(mechanism-oid-der-contents) || SSH-string(original-handshake-transcript-hash) || SSH-string(rejected-encuserauth) || SSH-string(sctx) )
section.t: The acceptor computes SshKeyFinished for that hash with the distinct role label "gss-sshkey acceptor retry v1" and the initiator nonce. This binds the retry to the session, the exact rejected attempt, and the reflected acceptor state. The initiator MUST verify this value before selecting another user key or signature algorithm.

section.name: Protocol Vectors
section.t: This vector fixes the DER and transcript encodings. Byte ranges use inclusive hexadecimal endpoints. Its inputs are:
section.sourcecode: mechanism-oid-der-contents = 2b06010401868d1f01 initiator-signature-algorithms = "ssh-ed25519,rsa-sha2-512" acceptor-signature-algorithms = "ssh-ed25519" initiator-ecdh-public-key = 00..1f acceptor-ecdh-public-key = 20..3f initiator-nonce = 40..5f acceptor-nonce = 60..7f acceptor-name = "sshkey@host.example" canonical-channel-bindings = 00 username = "alice" user-public-key-type = "ssh-ed25519" user-public-key-blob = 00010203 user-signature-algorithm = "ssh-ed25519" user-signature-blob = 040506
section.t: DER(SshKeyUserAuth), the handshake transcript hash, and SHA-256 of the complete user signature input are, respectively:

section.name: Initiator KEX Token
section.t: The first initiator token contains status SSH-KEY-CONTINUE-NEEDED and a SshKeyKEX value. The kextypes, enctypes, and sigtypes fields contain the initiator algorithm lists. The kextype, enctype, and pk fields SHOULD contain the initiator's preferred proposal. When pk is present, nonce and acceptorName MUST also be present. The first initiator token SHOULD NOT contain EncSshKeyUserAuth, because the initiator cannot encrypt user authentication until it has received the acceptor ECDH public key.

section.name: Acceptor-First KEX Token
section.t: GSS-API does not require the initiator to generate the first context-establishment token. If the acceptor is called first with no input token, it sends SSH-KEY-CONTINUE-NEEDED with SshKeyKEX, SshKeyHostAuth, and sctx. The token contains the acceptor's supported algorithms, preferred key-exchange public value, and a host-key signature over the acceptor-first challenge transcript. Because the initiator has not yet supplied a target name, the acceptor MUST obtain acceptorName from a named acceptor credential before producing this token.

The initiator response to an acceptor-first token contains its own SshKeyKEX value, EncSshKeyUserAuth, SshKeyFinished, and the reflected sctx. The acceptor uses sctx to recover its ephemeral ECDH state, derives the session key, decrypts the user authentication payload, validates the user signature, checks local authorization policy, and verifies the initiator finished MAC.

HTTP Negotiate is a natural acceptor-first deployment. An HTTP server MAY include an acceptor-first GSS-SSHKEY token in a 401 WWW-Authenticate header. The HTTP client can then return its ECDH public key, encrypted user authentication, key confirmation, and reflected sctx in the Authorization header. This lets the server authenticate the request during the normal HTTP authentication challenge round trip. If explicit acceptor key confirmation is required by the local implementation, the server can carry a final acceptor SshKeyFinished token in the HTTP response.

section.name: Acceptor KEX and Host Authentication Token
section.t: The acceptor validates the proposal, chooses algorithms, computes its key-exchange public value, and returns status SSH-KEY-CONTINUE-NEEDED. The returned token contains SshKeyKEX with the selected algorithms and acceptor public value, and a SshKeyHostAuth value containing a hostauth signature.

In initiator-first exchanges, the acceptor can derive the session key after receiving the initiator public key. The acceptor token therefore MAY also contain SshKeyFinished. The initiator verifies the selected algorithms, hostauth.sig, and host-key trust policy before completing the context.

section.name: Encrypted User Authentication
section.t: Once the initiator has the acceptor ECDH public key, it derives the session keys, computes the user signature described in , DER encodes SshKeyUserAuth, encrypts it as EncSshKeyUserAuth, and sends it in the next token. The same token SHOULD contain the initiator SshKeyFinished value and MUST return sctx unchanged when sctx was present in the acceptor token.

section.name: Completion Token
section.t: The acceptor decrypts encuserauth, validates the SSH user signature, authorizes the requested username, verifies the initiator finished MAC, and verifies that sctx is current. It then sets the accepted source name to the requested username and returns SSH-KEY-COMPLETE.

If the user signature is valid but that key is not authorized for the requested username, the acceptor MAY return SSH-KEY-CONTINUE-NEEDED. This retry token contains negotiation-form SshKeyKEX with the original acceptor sigtypes, the unchanged sctx, and the retry SshKeyFinished described in . It contains no hostauth, encuserauth, cctx, or key-exchange proposal. The initiator MUST verify all of these constraints and the retry Finished against its exact previous encuserauth before advancing to its next configured key and signature-algorithm candidate. Candidate exhaustion fails the context locally.
Invalid signatures, unadvertised algorithms, malformed tokens, failed freshness, and failed key confirmation are not retryable and fail context establishment.
A peer that receives SSH-KEY-FAILURE MUST fail context establishment and MUST discard all state derived from the failed exchange.

section.name: Context State Tokens
section.t: The cctx and sctx fields carry encrypted context state for implementations that need stateless initiator or acceptor operation. cctx is state intended for the initiator. sctx is state intended for the acceptor.

Context state MUST be confidentiality and integrity protected using keys unavailable to the peer that stores or reflects the state. Long-term private keys MUST NOT be stored in cctx or sctx. Context state MUST include the key-exchange transcript values and an authenticated issuedAt Unix time. The acceptor MUST apply a local maximum-age policy to issuedAt and reject missing or malformed values. An acceptor MAY tolerate limited future skew to accommodate clock differences between acceptors sharing a context-protection key. For acceptor continuations, sctx MUST contain enough encrypted state for another acceptor process with the same context-protection key to finish authentication. This state MUST include acceptorName so a continuation cannot be moved to a different acceptor audience.

The local age limit bounds but does not eliminate replay. Without a fresh carrier binding or external single-use state, a completed stateless exchange is a bearer token while the acceptor's local age policy accepts issuedAt. This specification does not require a replay cache because availability and coordination of such state are deployment properties. A future integration may let a carrier explicitly accept responsibility for replay mitigation, for example when TLS already provides an encrypted channel.
In the acceptor-first flow, sctx contains the acceptor's ephemeral ECDH private key until the initiator returns its public key. Long-term SSH host or user private keys MUST NOT be stored in sctx.

section.name: Per-Message Tokens
section.t: After SSH-KEY-COMPLETE, gss_get_mic(), gss_verify_mic(), gss_wrap(), and gss_unwrap() use CFX token framing and the RFC 8009 AES128-CTS-HMAC-SHA256-128 profile. K_base is the profile protocol key. RFC 4121 key usages 22 and 23 protect tokens sent by the acceptor; usages 24 and 25 protect tokens sent by the initiator. Sequence numbers start at zero in each direction.

A receiver authenticates a token before classifying its sequence number. Authenticated duplicate, old, reordered, and gap tokens return the corresponding GSS supplementary status while retaining the authenticated output, as required by GSS-API.

section.name: Error Handling
section.t: SSH-KEY-FAILURE is a generic protocol failure. A future version may define structured error codes. Until then, implementations SHOULD expose local diagnostic details through GSS minor status values rather than placing unauthenticated details on the wire.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: IANA is requested to assign one new entry from the "SMI Security for Mechanism Codes" registry under iso.org.dod.internet.security.mechanisms (1.3.6.1.5.5):
section.sourcecode: Value: TBD1 Name: sshkey Description: SSH Public-Key GSS-API Mechanism Reference: This document, Section 3
section.t: The assigned value replaces TBD1 in . The private implementation OID shown there is not requested for registration.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The security of this mechanism depends on correct validation of SSH host public keys and correct authorization of SSH user public keys. Implementations MUST NOT accept unknown host keys merely because they can verify hostauth.sig.

Signature inputs bind the algorithm lists, selected algorithms, and key-exchange public values. The finished MAC binds the derived session key to the same transcript. Omitting these values can permit downgrade, unknown-key-share, or key-confirmation failures.

EncSshKeyUserAuth hides the username, user public key, and user signature from passive observers. To reduce active identity probing, initiator implementations SHOULD validate the acceptor host signature and host-key trust policy before sending EncSshKeyUserAuth when that policy information is available locally. In all cases, implementations MUST NOT report a mutually authenticated context unless host-key policy succeeds.
Every AES-CTS encryption requires a fresh, unpredictable 16-octet confounder. An implementation MUST fail rather than emit an encrypted field or sealed per-message token if its random source fails.

Context state tokens are especially sensitive. They MUST be integrity protected and bound to the key-exchange transcript values, acceptor audience, and issuance time. Local maximum-age policy limits only the replay window. A completed token remains reusable while that policy accepts it unless the carrier mitigates replay. Implementations MUST document this property and MUST NOT describe age checking alone as single-use replay protection.

A DNS hostname for the initiator is not authenticated by this mechanism and MUST NOT be used for local authorization, as specified in . Reverse DNS does not turn a transport source address into an authenticated initiator identity.
This draft intentionally uses a private experimental OID. Deploying that OID outside controlled experiments risks collision with other private uses.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: The repository associated with this draft currently implements the mechanism loader interface for Heimdal and MIT krb5, SAnon-compatible X25519 key derivation, SSH signature blob handling, encrypted acceptor continuation state, client-first and acceptor-first context establishment, RFC 4121-style per-message protection, and focused OpenSSH configuration and authorized_keys policy. Repeatable tests cover loader interoperability, authenticated context establishment, and per-message protection. Direct OpenSSH client and server integration remains implementation work.

section.name: ASN.1 Module
section.t: This module is normative for context-establishment token syntax.
